mentions.context: Subs adopt the GC's platform through gritted teeth, and that attitude flows into the data

mentions.context: The integrator is the durable role in a stack no single vendor can serve

mentions.context: A world where every owner Frankensteins their own platform is worse than the platform monopoly

mentions.context: You are increasingly paying for a UI you will interface with less and less

mentions.context: Customer success churn at a vendor is an adoption risk, not just an annoyance

mentions.context: Acquisition is a defensive move that makes the buying environment worse for contractors

mentions.context: Palantir's product is the ontology, and dashboards are just the surface

mentions.context: AI will make commissioning agents more efficient, not replace them, it's only as good as the human's prompt

mentions.quote: I'm a little more skeptical of our AI utopia future. One thing I've observed is you can't automate what you don't understand. I think our first threshold condition is going to be augmentation, not replacement. And that augmentation phase will be a long one.

mentions.context: A GPT-to-vibe-code-to-architect-mode pipeline compresses the product dev cycle

mentions.context: Match the AI model to the job: ChatGPT to spar, Claude to edit, Gemini to research

mentions.context: Firms that lean into AI to make PMs' lives less sucky will win the talent war within a decade

mentions.context: AI submittal review acts as a robot mentor that teaches juniors what to look for

mentions.context: The IP of a construction company is its people, when owners evaluate a bid they are really interviewing the project team, and even global GCs win or lose work on relationships
mentions.quote: I truly believe the IP of construction is our people. When we bid on a job, yes, they wanna know our means and methods, but what they're really doing is they're interviewing our people... even we as a global company, deals are won or lost based off of relationships.

mentions.context: Capturing retiring superintendents' knowledge is a data-collection problem before it is an LLM problem, hallucinations make him wary of models over unstructured field knowledge, so the actionable…
mentions.quote: I've played around with ChatGPT and Copilot, Claude... and it does get hallucinations. So I'd be very worried about that... it's really about if we can scale up data collection now, and how do we download those people now?

mentions.context: Connected platforms linking digital tools to physical tools broke BIM out of 15 years of siloed workflows, and every break in the office-to-field information chain is an opportunity for risk.
mentions.quote: If we would not have seen tools like Revizto, tools like OpenSpace, tools like Dusty Robotics, just to name a few, we'd probably still be where we were 15 years ago with these siloed tools just kind of doing their thing.

mentions.context: Contractors are now building software to own the data, not to save the license fee
mentions.quote: It's not even so much that we're spending 300 grand and we're saving the money over the next couple years. That's not necessarily the play. It's we're spending 300 grand and we're basically creating a moat for ourselves as a company because it's our data now.

mentions.context: Subs adopt the GC's platform through gritted teeth, and that attitude flows into the data
mentions.quote: They're being forced to, but it's through gritted teeth and they hate it. The attitude down on my end is not great about those systems. So we're already trying to bend and having to do what the next customer wants us to do.

mentions.context: The integrator is the durable role in a stack no single vendor can serve
mentions.quote: No one company is going to be able to serve every single segment of the market... Procore doesn't necessarily work for, or ACC for that matter, doesn't work for a steel detailing workflow.

mentions.context: His CM Planner method strips drawings to a blank sheet in AutoCAD, rebuilds them layer-by-layer in build sequence with each layer matching a schedule task and green/yellow/red pass colors, and trades…
mentions.quote: Everybody seems to be able to relate to that better than the last planner system in my opinion, or takt planning or any of that stuff.

mentions.context: Web-based collaborative takeoff breaks the desktop silo of legacy tools
mentions.quote: What's so different about Togal is we're web-based. Legacy software is the on-screens, Bluebeams. If Jeremy has a takeoff bid that's due, he can share those plans with 10 of his estimators with a click of a button... none of that information is lost, it's all web based. So you don't have these silos.

mentions.context: Consolidation, not novel capability, converts practitioner skeptics: he MacGyvered drone capture with a $3 app seven years ago and only saw DroneDeploy's value once it collapsed two or three…
mentions.quote: Where I would have to use like two or three different platforms, it's all in one spot... overlaying plans onto drone images ,  I could figure out how to do it in Photoshop and [Bluebeam], but they have it just built into their platform now.

mentions.context: Palantir's product is the ontology, and dashboards are just the surface
mentions.quote: What they built is pretty stinking cool... but it's dashboarding. The subsurface is the ontology aspect of it. When you hear ontology, they're going to start trying to preach that out there like it's something that they invented. It's not.

mentions.context: Non-competing ConTech scale-ups are organizing a joint 'future of construction' conference (likely Austin) to replace separate vendor events that make customers travel all year.

mentions.guest: a Story the Field Believes with Jackie Guilbault
mentions.context: Contract value extends into the field, risk doesn't stop at signing
mentions.quote: You can negotiate the best contract in the world. But if you don't follow the terms that you negotiated initially or use it to your advantage, you don't always have to reach into your contingency budget for things. You can use the contract to your advantage.

mentions.guest: a Story the Field Believes with Jackie Guilbault
mentions.context: Founder-market fit: an ex-construction-attorney CEO builds for the persona's real pain
mentions.quote: What makes Document Crunch unique is our CEO came from the industry. He was a construction attorney. And so he intimately knows the pain that our persona is dealing with... the product is built for someone like him.

mentions.context: ConTech M&A is a data land-grab, not a product roll-up
mentions.quote: It's a data play from what I can tell. It's how much data have these companies captured that we can fold into our own ecosystem and use that to train the AI models on top of it.

mentions.context: Her WhatsApp group of female construction-tech founders has found only 13 worldwide so far, including Dusty Robotics and Versatile, a stark measure of how thin the founder pipeline is.
mentions.quote: I actually started the one with female founders in construction tech. Do you want to guess how many I found worldwide? ... 13 so far.

mentions.context: Robots widen the industry's talent base by making trades appealing to younger workers
mentions.quote: You can train a younger person who's effectively using a PlayStation controller and an iPad to run a robot that otherwise would be disinterested in doing drywall finishing... then you need the technical support to do the maintenance.

mentions.context: By 2030 a data center build will have 10+ robots, not for novelty but for cost, speed and safety
mentions.quote: Now is the moment where it's not too hard to paint a picture of having five, 10 plus robots on a job site. Not because we like technology, it's because it will help us deliver jobs faster, more effectively and cheaper and with less health and safety risks.

mentions.context: We asked AI if we're an AI company; 2 of 3 engines said yes
mentions.quote: We went to... three of the AI engines... ChatGPT, Copilot, Grok... and we prompted them, look at everything online about QNECT and tell us if we're already AI. And two out of three said that we were. So, are we an AI company? According to AI, we're an AI company.

mentions.context: Overusing ChatGPT for internal emails erodes your professional brand because people can tell
mentions.quote: 50 % of the emails I see now probably don't need to be emails... and you can tell they're copy pasted from chat GPT... don't take it for face value because you know when it's AI generated. So go out, connect with people, have conversations. Sitting down face to face is a hundred times more effective than an email that chat GPT or co-pilot helped you craft.

mentions.context: Microsoft-only shops are bringing in Claude alongside Copilot, and scaled workflow distribution is still the unsolved part
mentions.quote: I'm seeing a lot of Microsoft only shops bringing in Claude as their enterprise license... but even then, you start to run into issues with how can I pass these workflows out at scale. They're starting to solve some of those things by being able to share out skills, but even then it's a bit of a mess.

mentions.context: Every subcontractor runs change orders differently, mostly on Word, Excel, or paper
mentions.quote: The insight there was just like, oh, every single one does it differently. And it's mostly done on Microsoft Word or Excel, or if it's in the field, it's paper.

mentions.context: Digitalization mostly digitized the paper process, Word and Excel replicating paper forms, and lost the chance to improve the work itself; AI is the second chance to redesign processes rather than…
mentions.quote: Why do we have Word documents? Why do we have Excel spreadsheets? Well, that was the way we did it on paper. So we digitalized the paper process, but we lost the opportunity to actually make the process better by moving it to technology. So I think AI gives us the opportunity to actually repurpose technology to serve us.

mentions.context: Hire for problem-solving persistence, not AI proficiency, the tooling is already table stakes
mentions.quote: Not to oversimplify project management, but I always saw it as variable control and problem solving... Are they able to stick with a problem and solve it and see it all the way through? Are they okay interacting with other individuals?

mentions.context: Hyperscale data centers have achieved 'China-level speed', a giant microchip on the earth
mentions.quote: If you look at something like Stargate in Texas... he says we finally achieved China level speed. In some ways that's just a giant microchip on the surface of the earth. A lot of the constraints that we find in smaller projects just aren't there.

mentions.context: Optimal modularity sits on a diagonal: standardization must be matched to required flexibility
mentions.quote: Imagine a matrix. You have flexibility on one axis and standardization on the other axis, and the optimal modular solution lays out on a diagonal line. A substation is highly standardized... a prefab kitchen pod needs to be higher flexibility, but not as high as a custom home.

mentions.context: Every model and chip generation cuts cost per token by roughly an order of magnitude, and unprecedented data-center capex (~$650B/year from hyperscalers, near 2008-bailout scale) plus…
mentions.quote: Every time a model comes out and honestly, every time the chips come out, the cost per token goes down by like an order of magnitude... I do think it'll get so cheap that it won't be the major consideration.

mentions.context: The best ConTech customer support answers questions that have nothing to do with the software, domain expertise in CS is the moat
mentions.quote: When you call customer support at SmartPM, you might have a question on the principles of good project controls. How do I make sure I'm getting the most out of coordinating a schedule across all of my trades and with my owner at every OAC meeting? That question has nothing to do with the software and everything to do with the outcomes.

mentions.context: Back-office schedule updating is low-hanging fruit for agentic AI right now, a chat-based agent reconciling what should have happened against what did and adjusting tied activities should be…
mentions.quote: Schedule updates I think are like ripe for it... an agentic thing that just is chat based where it's like what should have happened, okay give me an update on what did happen... I feel like that should be something that should be able to be done now.

mentions.context: A GC's A-team or C-team is visible within 30 days, and the tell is a milestone schedule that is actually followed
mentions.quote: An A-team in the first 30 days looks like they have a very well thought out schedule. And I'm not talking about a real pretty P6 schedule. Come up with a really good milestone schedule that is actually followed. We have been in month eight without a schedule before. And I don't know how things get done, honestly.

mentions.context: Cloud value has stagnated because SaaS providers grew so many layers of customer success that people who never touched the problem are building for it, losing the developer-to-user intimacy that made…
mentions.quote: The cloud providers have become so big and there's so many layers of customer success that people who have never touched the problem [are] trying to solve a problem they don't understand. So we've actually gotten to a point where the efficiency or the value of cloud and digitalization, I feel, has stagnated.

mentions.context: The customer success model was pioneered by Salesforce as a subtle way of selling
mentions.quote: It's a model that was really pioneered by Salesforce in the early two thousands. What they found was when they put someone in charge of helping a customer achieve their goals, that the customer was more likely to achieve those goals... And it's a subtle way of selling.

mentions.context: Agents sitting on the database can replace SaaS business logic (per Satya Nadella), yet incumbents' real moats, relationships, trust, familiarity, are stronger than people think; what's genuinely…
mentions.quote: People are going to say, well, if I can string up an agent to do this for me, maybe I don't need 10 licenses. Maybe I just need two. Definitely why ServiceNow, Salesforce, and some of those other folks had a rough, rough week.

mentions.quote: They don't build airplanes. They don't build cars without modeling every single part of that vehicle, right? Because it goes into a factory and it gets built and automated. So maybe that's the missing link still. It's like how we consume information.

mentions.quote: Initially was a hack and then it became part of the product and it was really, really what allowed us to really more seamlessly connect model information to the field... making sure that information that we coordinated actually gets out there the field and gets built accurately.

And if we can get there, I'm excited for that future.

mentions.context: Architect construction software as a true network, not upstream/downstream portals
mentions.quote: Right after we launched, all the early feedback was like, this is awesome, but I want to use it upstream with my client and downstream with my subcontractors... we recognized early on that we had to re-architect the platform to be a true network. So we spent all of 2019 re-architecting the platform.

mentions.context: The real change order problem is exposure and visibility, not the T&M ticket
mentions.quote: T is just one part of the challenge and really it's change order exposure more broadly. How do I as a GC know everything that's out there that all of my subcontractors have sent me? And then all of a sudden, it was morphing into a much bigger platform and bigger problem set to go solve.

mentions.context: Map every manual step, then reverse-engineer what to automate
mentions.quote: So really it's just about mapping out every step that goes into this manual... we really mapped out what we thought was the industry best practice in every manual step. And then it was just kind of like reverse engineering. Like, what can we automate?

mentions.context: Specialty trades finance every change order themselves, labor and materials are paid before the change is even approved
mentions.quote: Most specialty trades, their cash flow is dictated based on how quickly they get paid for changes. You have to pay the overhead to payroll, the cost of the day and the cost of materials before the change is made. Then you record a time and materials ticket, that becomes an invoice, that invoice is sent to the general contractor, and there's almost always a conversation.

mentions.context: With Claude embedded in Excel and PowerPoint, AI accepts work the way people already do it instead of forcing SaaS-style structured input, let people work how they're comfortable and add intelligence…
mentions.quote: Some of the strictness that SaaS requires isn't required by AI... where you can give people the ability to work the way they're comfortable working and then add the value and intelligence on the back end. That's one way I think that we can really win.

mentions.context: Cut information until it hurts and give every slide a buddy in the appendix
mentions.quote: I don't think about what's all the information I need to put into this presentation. I think instead: what is the least amount of information I can present and still give a really strong presentation. You cut away information until it absolutely hurts... Every slide has a buddy. You put the full data set in the appendix and a footnote that says see appendix page 34.

mentions.context: Reading text-filled slides signals to the audience that you have nothing to add beyond the screen
mentions.quote: Adults can read... The bigger problem is we're signaling to our audience, I don't have anything of value to add for you beyond what you see on the screen. In which case the audience is thinking, can you please just email this to us?

mentions.context: ConTech founders obsess over perceived competitors while the vast industry sits unpenetrated, and daily decision divergence means perceived competitors end up in different places anyway.
mentions.quote: They were standing in a corner and looking into a ballroom, but the ballroom was the industry. But instead of looking into the ballroom, they were fighting each other in the corner.
